# Focus Detection Device: Detailed Description

## Overview of the Optical Configuration

The focus detection device is constructed around a plurality of micro-lenses arranged in a two-dimensional array pattern. This array is strategically positioned to receive light fluxes that have passed through an image forming optical system, such as a camera lens or similar imaging apparatus. Each micro-lens within this array functions as a discrete optical element, capturing a specific angular and spatial segment of the incoming light field. By arranging these micro-lenses in a two-dimensional grid, the device is able to sample the light field across the entire image plane in both horizontal and vertical directions, thereby providing comprehensive coverage of the subject image projected by the optical system.

## Light Receiving Element Configuration

In correspondence with each individual micro-lens, a plurality of light receiving elements is disposed to capture the light fluxes transmitted through that particular micro-lens. This arrangement means that every micro-lens has its own dedicated cluster or group of light receiving elements positioned beneath it, effectively creating a micro-lens-to-sensor-array correspondence throughout the entire device. Each light receiving element within a given cluster captures light that has traveled through a distinct sub-region of the exit pupil of the image forming optical system. As a result, the light receiving elements associated with each micro-lens collectively record multiple perspectives of the same point on the subject, differentiated by the angle at which the light entered the optical system. This configuration is fundamental to enabling both phase difference detection and subject image analysis, as it preserves directional information about the incoming light that would otherwise be lost in conventional imaging sensors.

## Focus Detection Through Phase Difference Analysis

Based on the outputs generated by the light receiving elements, a focus detection unit is provided to determine the defocus quantity of the image forming optical system. This determination is achieved through analysis of the phase difference between light fluxes originating from different areas—specifically, different regions of the exit pupil of the optical system. Since the light receiving elements beneath each micro-lens capture light from distinct pupil regions, the focus detection unit can compare the relative positions or shifts of corresponding image signals derived from these different regions. When the optical system is precisely focused, light fluxes from different pupil areas converge at the same point, resulting in matching signal patterns. Conversely, when defocus is present, a measurable phase shift occurs between the signals corresponding to different pupil regions, and the magnitude and direction of this shift directly correlates to the amount and direction of defocus. Through this phase difference detection methodology, the focus detection unit is able to calculate the precise defocus quantity of the image forming optical system.

## Recognition of Subject Image Characteristics

In addition to the focus detection unit, the device further comprises a recognition unit configured to identify characteristics of the subject image formed on the light receiving elements via the micro-lenses. This recognition unit utilizes the same outputs from the light receiving elements that are used for defocus detection, thereby leveraging the captured data for a dual purpose. The characteristics identified by the recognition unit may include, but are not limited to, spatial frequency content of the subject, contrast levels, brightness distribution, the presence of repetitive patterns, edge orientations, color information, and other distinguishing features inherent to the subject image. By analyzing these characteristics, the recognition unit effectively creates a profile or classification of the type of subject being captured, which provides critical contextual information that can influence the reliability and accuracy of different defocus detection approaches.

## Adaptive Optimization of Defocus Detection

The focus detection unit is further configured to adapt its defocus detection method to achieve optimal performance based on the subject image characteristics identified by the recognition unit. This adaptive capability represents a significant advancement over conventional focus detection systems, which typically apply a single, fixed algorithm regardless of the nature of the subject being photographed. Because different subject characteristics—such as low contrast, repetitive patterns, or fine detail—can each present unique challenges to phase difference detection, the ability to dynamically select or adjust the detection methodology in response to recognized subject characteristics substantially improves the accuracy and reliability of the focus detection process. For instance, when the recognition unit identifies a subject with low contrast, the focus detection unit may adjust its algorithm to apply enhanced signal processing techniques suited for such conditions. Alternatively, when a repetitive pattern is detected, the focus detection unit may select a detection method specifically designed to avoid erroneous phase difference calculations that could otherwise arise from pattern periodicity. Through this feedback-driven, adaptive relationship between the recognition unit and the focus detection unit, the overall device achieves a higher degree of precision and robustness in determining defocus quantity across a diverse range of shooting conditions and subject types.

# Focus Detection Device with Adaptive Subject Recognition

## Background and Overview

Modern imaging systems, including digital cameras and optical instruments, require precise and rapid focus detection to produce sharp, well-defined images across a wide range of shooting conditions and subject types. Traditional focus detection systems often rely on a single, fixed method of analyzing incoming light to determine focus accuracy, which can lead to suboptimal performance when subject matter varies significantly—for example, when photographing a fast-moving object, a low-contrast scene, a repetitive pattern, or a subject with complex textures. To address these limitations, an advanced focus detection device has been developed that combines high-precision phase-difference detection with intelligent subject recognition capabilities, allowing the system to adapt its detection strategy in real time based on the nature of the image being captured.

## Structural Configuration

At the core of this focus detection device is a two-dimensional array of micro-lenses, each precisely aligned with and optically coupled to a corresponding light receiving element. This micro-lens array is strategically positioned within the optical path of an image forming optical system, such that light entering through different regions or areas of the main imaging lens is directed by the micro-lenses onto specific, designated light receiving elements. This arrangement effectively partitions the incoming light flux according to its point of origin within the aperture of the optical system, enabling the device to independently sample and analyze light that has traveled through distinct zones of the lens.

The light receiving elements, which may be implemented as photodiodes, charge-coupled devices (CCDs), or complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) sensor elements, convert the incoming optical signals into electrical output signals. These output signals serve two critical and simultaneous functions within the device, forming the basis of its dual-capability design.

## Phase-Difference Defocus Detection

The first function of the light receiving element outputs is to enable detection of the defocus quantity of the image forming optical system through a phase-difference detection methodology. Because the two-dimensional micro-lens array allows light from different areas of the optical system's exit pupil to be captured separately, the device can compare the relative phase, or positional alignment, of the light flux patterns received from these different areas.

When the image forming optical system is precisely focused on the subject, light rays originating from different areas of the lens aperture will converge at the same point on the image plane, resulting in matching or well-aligned signal patterns among corresponding light receiving elements. Conversely, when the optical system is out of focus—whether in a front-focus or back-focus condition—the light flux patterns from different aperture areas will exhibit a measurable positional shift or phase difference relative to one another. By analyzing the magnitude and direction of this phase difference across the two-dimensional array, the focus detection device can precisely calculate both the amount and direction of defocus, providing the information necessary to drive an autofocus mechanism toward accurate focus position.

## Subject Image Characteristic Recognition

Simultaneously with the phase-difference defocus calculation, the same output signals from the light receiving elements are utilized by the device to recognize and characterize features of the subject image itself. Because the two-dimensional array captures spatially resolved information about the scene, the device can analyze patterns such as contrast levels, brightness distribution, edge sharpness, repetitive structures, color information (if applicable), and the general spatial frequency content of the subject.

This recognition process allows the focus detection device to classify or characterize the subject image according to various criteria—for instance, distinguishing between a high-contrast subject and a low-contrast subject, identifying repetitive or periodic patterns that might otherwise confuse phase-difference calculations, detecting low-light or low-signal conditions, or recognizing subjects with predominantly horizontal or vertical structural elements. The device essentially performs a form of real-time scene analysis using the very same light receiving element outputs that are employed for defocus detection, thereby eliminating the need for additional sensors or a separate image analysis subsystem.

## Adaptive Detection Method Selection

The most significant advantage of this dual-capability design lies in its ability to leverage the recognized subject image characteristics to dynamically select and apply the most appropriate focus detection method for the given situation. Rather than relying on a single, universal algorithm for phase-difference calculation regardless of scene content, the focus detection unit can adjust its processing approach based on what it has learned about the subject.

For example, if the recognition process identifies that the subject has low contrast, the device may select a detection algorithm optimized for extracting subtle phase differences from weak signal variations, potentially incorporating additional signal amplification or noise-reduction techniques. If the subject exhibits a repetitive pattern that could otherwise produce ambiguous or erroneous phase-difference readings due to pattern aliasing, the device can switch to an alternative detection method less susceptible to such errors, or it may select a different pairing of light receiving elements across the array to avoid the problematic spatial frequencies. Similarly, in cases where the recognized subject characteristics indicate uneven illumination or partial occlusion, the device can prioritize data from specific regions of the micro-lens array that provide more reliable phase information, effectively ignoring or de-weighting unreliable signal areas.

This adaptive selection process may be governed by a control unit or processor integrated within the focus detection device, which receives the subject characteristic data, compares it against predetermined criteria or reference patterns, and subsequently activates the corresponding optimal detection algorithm or parameter set. The control unit may also be configured to learn from previous focus detection attempts, refining its selection criteria over time to further improve performance.

## Advantages and Applications

By integrating subject recognition directly into the focus detection process, this device achieves several important advantages over conventional focus detection systems. First, it significantly enhances the accuracy of defocus detection across a diverse range of shooting conditions, since the detection algorithm is no longer a fixed, one-size-fits-all approach but rather one that is tailored to the specific characteristics of the scene being captured. Second, it improves the adaptability and robustness of the autofocus system, allowing it to perform reliably even when confronted with challenging subjects that might otherwise cause conventional phase-difference systems to produce inaccurate or unstable focus readings. Third, because both the defocus calculation and subject recognition functions rely on the same underlying array of light receiving elements, the device achieves this enhanced performance without requiring substantial additional hardware, keeping the overall system compact, cost-effective, and efficient in terms of power consumption and processing resources.

This focus detection device is well-suited for incorporation into a wide variety of imaging systems, including digital single-lens reflex cameras, mirrorless cameras, video recording equipment, industrial inspection systems, and other optical instruments where rapid, accurate, and adaptable focus detection is essential to overall system performance.

# Focus Detection: The Foundation of Sharp Imaging

Focus detection is a critical technology used in cameras, optical instruments, and imaging systems to determine whether a subject is properly focused and to guide adjustments for achieving sharp, clear images. This process forms the backbone of autofocus (AF) systems found in modern digital cameras, smartphones, camcorders, and even scientific instruments like microscopes and telescopes.

## How Focus Detection Works

At its core, focus detection analyzes the image formed by a lens system to identify the point at which light rays converge most precisely on the sensor or film plane. When an image is out of focus, light rays from a single point on the subject spread out into a blurred circle rather than converging to a sharp point. Focus detection systems are designed to measure this blur and provide feedback that drives the lens elements to the correct position.

## Main Types of Focus Detection

**Contrast Detection**
This method examines the image sensor data directly, measuring the contrast between adjacent pixels. As the lens moves through its focus range, the system continuously evaluates contrast levels—sharper images produce higher contrast at edges and details. The system searches for the point of maximum contrast, indicating optimal focus. While highly accurate, this method can be relatively slow since it requires iterative adjustments.

**Phase Detection**
Phase detection systems split incoming light into pairs of images and compare their alignment. By analyzing the phase difference between these separated light paths, the system can calculate not only whether the image is out of focus but also the direction and amount of adjustment needed. This allows for significantly faster focusing compared to contrast detection, making it ideal for tracking moving subjects.

**Hybrid Systems**
Many modern cameras combine both phase and contrast detection methods to leverage the speed of phase detection with the precision of contrast detection. These hybrid autofocus systems are particularly common in mirrorless cameras and smartphones, offering both quick initial focus acquisition and fine-tuned accuracy.

**Time-of-Flight and Laser-Assisted Detection**
Some advanced systems use infrared or laser sensors to measure the distance to a subject directly, bypassing traditional optical analysis. This approach is especially useful in low-light conditions where contrast and phase detection may struggle.

## Applications

Focus detection technology extends far beyond consumer photography. It plays a vital role in:

- **Medical imaging**, ensuring diagnostic scans capture clear details
- **Industrial inspection**, where precise focus is necessary for quality control
- **Astronomical observation**, allowing telescopes to lock onto distant celestial objects
- **Robotics and machine vision**, enabling automated systems to interpret their surroundings accurately

## Challenges and Advancements

Despite significant progress, focus detection systems face ongoing challenges, including performance in low-light environments, tracking fast-moving subjects, and handling low-contrast scenes such as plain walls or overcast skies. Manufacturers continue to innovate with AI-powered subject recognition, eye and face detection, and predictive algorithms that anticipate motion patterns to maintain focus on moving targets.

## Conclusion

Focus detection represents a sophisticated blend of optics, sensor technology, and computational analysis. As imaging technology continues to evolve, these systems are becoming faster, more accurate, and more intelligent—capable of distinguishing between subjects, predicting movement, and operating reliably across diverse and challenging conditions. This continuous advancement ensures that photographers, scientists, and engineers alike can capture the sharp, precise images essential to their work.

A focus detection device for an imaging apparatus, comprising:

a microlens array comprising a plurality of microlenses arranged in a two-dimensional pattern, each microlens configured to receive light from a corresponding region of an imaging optical system's exit pupil;

a photoelectric conversion sensor disposed beneath the microlens array, comprising a plurality of pixel pairs, each pixel pair corresponding to a respective microlens and configured to output a pair of image signals representing light fluxes passing through different pupil regions of the imaging optical system;

a phase difference calculation unit configured to calculate a phase difference between the pair of image signals output from each pixel pair, and to calculate a defocus amount of the imaging optical system based on the calculated phase difference and a base-line length corresponding to a distance between the different pupil regions;

a subject recognition module configured to analyze image data acquired via the imaging optical system to identify a category of a subject present within an imaging field, the category being selected from among a plurality of predetermined subject categories including at least a human face, a human eye, an animal, and a moving object; and

a control unit configured to adaptively select or adjust a phase difference detection method used by the phase difference calculation unit, based on the subject category identified by the subject recognition module,

wherein the adaptive selection or adjustment includes at least one of:
(a) changing a combination of pixel pairs used for the phase difference calculation among a plurality of pixel pair groupings corresponding to different pupil-division directions,
(b) changing a size or shape of a focus detection area within the imaging field over which the pixel pairs are selected for the phase difference calculation,
(c) changing a correlation calculation algorithm or a weighting applied to the pair of image signals used in the phase difference calculation, and
(d) changing a reliability determination criterion applied to the calculated defocus amount,

such that the defocus amount is calculated using a detection method adapted to characteristics of the identified subject category.

---

**Claim 2** (dependent)

The focus detection device according to claim 1, wherein the subject recognition module is further configured to detect a distance or a movement direction of the identified subject relative to the imaging apparatus, and the control unit is configured to further adjust the phase difference detection method based on the detected distance or movement direction.

The focus detection device according to claim 1, wherein, when the subject recognition module identifies a human eye as the subject category, the control unit selects a focus detection area substantially coincident with a position of the identified human eye and increases a weighting applied to a pixel pair grouping corresponding to a pupil-division direction aligned with an eye contour.

The focus detection device according to claim 1, wherein, when the subject recognition module identifies a moving object as the subject category, the control unit selects a correlation calculation algorithm employing a shorter integration time or a predictive calculation based on a plurality of previously calculated defocus amounts.

The focus detection device according to claim 1, further comprising a lens driving unit configured to drive a focus lens of the imaging optical system based on the defocus amount calculated by the phase difference calculation unit, wherein the control unit is further configured to adjust a driving speed or a driving algorithm of the lens driving unit based on the identified subject category.

# Patent Claim: Autofocus System with Micro-Lens Array and Subject Recognition

## Claim 1

An autofocus system for an imaging apparatus, comprising:

a two-dimensional micro-lens array comprising a plurality of micro-lenses arranged in a matrix configuration across an image plane, each micro-lens configured to receive incident light from a photographic subject through an imaging optical system;

a plurality of light receiving elements optically coupled to said micro-lens array, wherein each micro-lens of said two-dimensional micro-lens array corresponds to a discrete group of light receiving elements among said plurality of light receiving elements, said light receiving elements being configured to generate a plurality of pairs of image signals corresponding to light fluxes passing through different pupil regions of the imaging optical system, for each of the plurality of micro-lenses;

a subject characteristic recognition unit configured to analyze image data derived from said plurality of light receiving elements to identify at least one characteristic of the photographic subject, said at least one characteristic being selected from the group consisting of: subject distance distribution, subject contrast pattern, subject spatial frequency content, subject motion, subject type, and subject region boundaries within an imaging field;

a selection unit, operatively connected to said subject characteristic recognition unit, configured to select, based on said at least one characteristic identified by said subject characteristic recognition unit, a subset of said plurality of micro-lenses and corresponding light receiving elements to be used for defocus calculation, and further configured to determine a calculation parameter for said defocus calculation based on said at least one characteristic; and

a defocus calculation unit configured to calculate a defocus amount of the imaging optical system based on a phase difference between the pairs of image signals obtained from the selected subset of light receiving elements, using the calculation parameter determined by said selection unit,

wherein said autofocus system adjusts a focus position of the imaging optical system based on the defocus amount calculated by said defocus calculation unit.

## Claim 2 (Dependent)

The autofocus system according to claim 1, wherein said calculation parameter includes at least one of a correlation calculation range, a weighting coefficient applied to the pairs of image signals, and a reliability threshold for the calculated defocus amount.

## Claim 3 (Dependent)

The autofocus system according to claim 1, wherein said subject characteristic recognition unit is configured to detect a human face or human eye within the imaging field, and said selection unit preferentially selects micro-lenses and corresponding light receiving elements associated with a region of the detected human face or human eye.

## Claim 4 (Dependent)

The autofocus system according to claim 1, wherein said subject characteristic recognition unit determines a contrast evaluation value for each of a plurality of divided regions corresponding to said two-dimensional micro-lens array, and said selection unit excludes from the defocus calculation those micro-lenses corresponding to divided regions having a contrast evaluation value below a predetermined threshold.

## Claim 5 (Dependent)

The autofocus system according to claim 1, wherein each of said light receiving elements corresponding to a given micro-lens comprises a plurality of photoelectric conversion sections arranged to receive light fluxes that have passed through mutually different partial pupil regions of an exit pupil of the imaging optical system, thereby enabling generation of the pairs of image signals without a dedicated phase-difference detection optical system separate from an imaging optical system.

## Claim 6 (Dependent)

The autofocus system according to claim 1, wherein said subject characteristic recognition unit comprises a memory storing a plurality of reference patterns corresponding to predetermined subject types, and a comparison circuit configured to compare the image data derived from said plurality of light receiving elements against said reference patterns to identify the subject type.

## Claim 7 (Dependent)

The autofocus system according to claim 1, wherein said selection unit is further configured to dynamically update the subset of selected micro-lenses and corresponding light receiving elements in response to a detected change in the at least one characteristic of the photographic subject over a plurality of successive image frames, so as to track a moving subject.
